entities.name: Dalmatius
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Dalmatius (c. 320 CE – 337 CE), a nephew of Emperor Constantine I, was briefly elevated to the rank of Caesar in the Roman Empire, a pivotal figure whose short life illuminates the complex dynastic politics and brutal succession struggles of the Constantinian dynasty. Born in Toulouse, his existence was intrinsically linked to the ambitions of his imperial uncle and the volatile political climate that followed the establishment of Christianity as a favored religion within the Roman state. His elevation to Caesar, alongside his half-brother Hannibalianus, represented Constantine's attempt to establish a clear line of succession, yet ironically paved the way for a bloody purge that would define the post-Constantinian era.

Appointed Caesar on September 18, 335 CE, Dalmatius was entrusted with the crucial task of defending the Danubian frontier, specifically Thrace, Macedonia, and Achaea, from Gothic incursions. His military command saw him engage with the Goths, who frequently threatened the empire's northern borders, demonstrating a brief but active role in Roman defense strategy. This appointment was part of Constantine's broader reorganization of the empire, dividing territories among his sons and nephews, with Dalmatius positioned to control vital strategic regions and act as a bulwark against barbarian incursions.

Dalmatius's promising, albeit brief, imperial career was abruptly terminated in 337 CE, shortly after the death of Constantine the Great. He was executed in the widespread purges that followed his uncle's demise, a brutal consolidation of power orchestrated primarily by Constantine's three surviving sons: Constantine II, Constantius II, and Constans. These purges eliminated numerous collateral relatives, including Dalmatius and Hannibalianus, ensuring that direct Constantinian lineage alone inherited the imperial throne. His death underscored the precarious nature of power within the Roman Empire, even for those within the imperial family.
